name: Cody Wylie
blurb: Cody Wylie (Republican, Rock Springs): Construction manager; Wyoming House District 39, 2023–Present. Unopposed in the Aug. 18, 2026 Republican primary for State House District 39.
background: Cody Wylie was born in Rock Springs, Wyoming. He earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Wyoming in 2011. His career experience includes working as a construction manager. As of 2022, Wylie served on the Rock Springs planning and zoning board.
Bio from my website is fine.

positions.topic: What are the biggest challenges and opportunities facing Wyoming today? As a legislator, how would you address them?
positions.text: Wyoming’s biggest challenge is creating opportunities for future generations while protecting the industries and values that define us. Energy, mining, agriculture, and construction remain vital, and we must support them while responsibly diversifying our economy. We can grow without losing what makes Wyoming special. …

positions.topic: We asked WyoFile readers to rank issues that are important to them, and healthcare costs and access topped the list. What can the Legislature do to make healthcare more affordable and accessible to Wyomingites?
positions.text: Healthcare affordability and access are challenges for families across Wyoming, especially in rural communities. We must ensure our rural hospitals, clinics and providers remain viable so Wyomingites can access care close to home. …

positions.topic: Do you support efforts to sell or transfer public land in Wyoming? How do you plan to ensure that state and federal land is managed in the best interest of the people of Wyoming?
positions.text: For the most part, I believe in keeping public lands in public hands. Growing up in southwest Wyoming has taught me there can be exceptions, but they should be limited, practical, and locally driven. When communities need room to grow, there should be a reasonable process for acquiring small parcels of public land. …

positions.topic: No two Wyoming counties are the same when it comes to how they generate revenue. As a legislator, how would you approach the public's desire for property tax relief with local revenue needs?
positions.text: Wyoming's counties are not all the same, and a one size fits all approach to property tax relief can create unintended consequences. …

positions.topic: What role, if any, should the Wyoming Legislature play in economic development?
positions.text: The Wyoming Legislature has an important role in economic development, but government should be a partner, not the driving force. Our job is to maintain a tax and regulatory environment that encourages investment, job creation, and long-term growth. …

positions.topic: Explain your values when it comes to campaign donations. Does Wyoming's system for monitoring campaign donations and expenditures need reform?
positions.text: Transparency in campaign donations is essential. Voters should know where candidates’ funding comes from to make informed decisions. Wyoming’s system offers some transparency, but it can be improved. The Legislature should continue reviewing it thoughtfully. …

name: Mike Yin
blurb: Mike Yin (Democratic, Jackson): Software Developer; Wyoming House District 16, 2019–Present. Unopposed in the Aug. 18, 2026 Democratic primary for State House District 16.
background: Mike Yin earned a bachelor's degree in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2007. Yin’s career experience includes working as a senior software developer with Android.

I am a software engineer and small business owner, and I have had the honor of representing the most of the Town of Jackson in the Wyoming House since 2019, currently serving as House Minority Leader. I earned a computer science degree from Carnegie Mellon and spent a decade writing software before running for office.

positions.topic: What are the biggest challenges and opportunities facing Wyoming today? As a legislator, how would you address them?
positions.text: Polarization has kept us from working on Wyoming. It has kept us from ensuring communities can thrive. It has threatened our access to the outdoors. And it has brought the vitriol from DC to Wyoming. As Minority Leader I work across the aisle, because supporting Wyoming's communities has never been a partisan project.

positions.topic: We asked WyoFile readers to rank issues that are important to them, and healthcare costs and access topped the list. What can the Legislature do to make healthcare more affordable and accessible to Wyomingites?
positions.text: The single most effective thing we could do is still pass Medicaid Expansion. Even after HR1, it would still reduce much of our uncompensated care which essentially gets passed on to all other payers.

positions.topic: Do you support efforts to sell or transfer public land in Wyoming? How do you plan to ensure that state and federal land is managed in the best interest of the people of Wyoming?
positions.text: No.

positions.topic: No two Wyoming counties are the same when it comes to how they generate revenue. As a legislator, how would you approach the public's desire for property tax relief with local revenue needs?
positions.text: The public passed "Amendment A" to allow us to tax primary homes differently from other properties. Instead of implementing the option the citizens of Wyoming gave us, we've made an endless confusing shotgun approach to relief. …

positions.topic: What role, if any, should the Wyoming Legislature play in economic development?
positions.text: If we truly believe in thriving communities and ensuring our kids can grow up and start a business or find a great career, we will need to be part of making that happen.

positions.topic: Explain your values when it comes to campaign donations. Does Wyoming's system for monitoring campaign donations and expenditures need reform?
positions.text: Yes. The people should know who spends money on our elections.

name: CJ Young
blurb: CJ Young (Republican, Cheyenne): Businessman; U.S. Navy Reserve. Lost the Aug. 18, 2026 Republican primary for Secretary of State with 15.3% of the vote.
background: Charles Young served in the U.S. Navy Reserve. Young completed his high school studies as a homeschooled student. He went on to earn an associate degree from Western Wyoming Community College in 2007 and a law degree from the University of Wyoming in 2014. Young's career experience includes working as a businessman.

For over a decade, I have served Wyoming in vital public roles. As former State Elections Director, I partnered with county clerks to administer secure, reliable elections. My service includes the Department of Corrections, acting as Military/Veterans Liaison for our congressional delegation, and serving as a U.S. Navy Reserve officer. As a local business owner, I know the need for efficient government and taxpayer stewardship. I’m running for SOS to deliver a professional, transparent office. I will strengthen election security, improve overseas military voting, support vet-owned businesses, and modernize services with absolute accountability.
education: High school: Homeschooled; Associates: Western Wyoming Community College, 2007; Law: University of Wyoming, 2014

positions.topic: Lawmakers have spent a lot of time in recent years considering and enacting changes to the state’s election system. As the state’s chief elections officer, what additional changes, if any, would you support?
positions.text: Wyoming elections are among the best in the nation, but we must always work to make them better. As Secretary of State, my focus will be on practical, data-driven security enhancements rather than political theater. I support targeted changes that make our elections easy to vote legally but hard to cheat. …

positions.topic: What do you believe is the appropriate role, if any, for the federal government to play in the administration or oversight of Wyoming’s elections? How willing would you be to work with the federal government in the expansion of that role?
positions.text: The United States Constitution leaves the administration of elections explicitly to the states. I firmly oppose any federal overreach or attempts to implement federally controlled elections. Wyoming knows how to run Wyoming elections best, and that authority belongs strictly with our state and our local county clerks. …

positions.topic: The secretary of state’s office works closely with Wyoming’s county clerks to oversee election administration. That relationship has been strained in recent years. How would you approach working with the county clerks?
positions.text: Having served as Wyoming’s State Elections Director, I know firsthand that secure, successful elections depend entirely on a strong partnership between the state and our 23 county clerks. The current strain in this relationship serves no one. …

positions.topic: What are the benefits and harms associated with Wyoming's minimal regulation of businesses registered in the state? What reforms would you recommend?
positions.text: Wyoming’s business-friendly environment is a cornerstone of our economy, attracting entrepreneurs nationwide and generating vital state revenue. The benefit of our low-regulation framework is that it encourages innovation, cuts red tape, and makes it simple to launch a business. …

positions.topic: How would you rate Wyoming’s existing system for monitoring campaign donations and expenditures? What, if any, changes would you pursue?
positions.text: Wyoming’s campaign finance system currently operates a bit like a paper tiger. While we have strict disclosure rules on the books, our enforcement and oversight capabilities are lacking. Under the Constitution, it is strictly the role of the Legislature to determine campaign finance laws and enact statutory changes. …

positions.topic: To what extent should the State Loan and Investment Board coordinate with local governments when it comes to state-sanctioned uses of state trust lands?
positions.text: As a member of the State Loan and Investment Board, my primary constitutional duty is to manage state trust lands to generate optimal, sustainable revenue for our public schools. However, maximizing revenue must not happen at the expense of our local communities. …

occupation: Educator (31 years; 20 in Campbell County School District)
background: I have been an educator for 31 years with 20 being in the Campbell County School District.

positions.topic: What are the biggest challenges and opportunities facing Wyoming today? As a legislator, how would you address them?
positions.text: As a legislator, I’ll tackle rural healthcare by backing smart, stable funding that keeps our local clinics and hospitals open without hitting property owners with higher taxes. …

positions.topic: We asked WyoFile readers to rank issues that are important to them, and healthcare costs and access topped the list. What can the Legislature do to make healthcare more affordable and accessible to Wyomingites?
positions.text: To make healthcare more affordable, we have to cut through the red tape and look at practical solutions. First, we need to take a hard look at prescription drug costs. By forcing more transparency on pharmacy benefit managers, we can make sure discounts actually get passed down to folks at the pharmacy counter. …

positions.topic: Do you support efforts to sell or transfer public land in Wyoming? How do you plan to ensure that state and federal land is managed in the best interest of the people of Wyoming?
positions.text: When it comes to our public lands, I’m 100% against selling or transferring them to private interests. These spaces are a massive part of Wyoming's heritage, tourism, and outdoor lifestyle. …

positions.topic: No two Wyoming counties are the same when it comes to how they generate revenue. As a legislator, how would you approach the public's desire for property tax relief with local revenue needs?
positions.text: Balancing property tax relief with local revenue needs is all about finding a middle ground. We need to protect homeowners without cutting the legs out from under the vital services our counties rely on, like our local law enforcement, emergency services, and roads. …

positions.topic: What role, if any, should the Wyoming Legislature play in economic development?
positions.text: The Legislature definitely has a big role to play in economic development, but it shouldn't be about the state picking winners and losers with your tax dollars. Instead, our job is to build a rock-solid foundation so local businesses can thrive and new industries actually want to set up shop here.

positions.text: I truly feel that the system we have in place right now works well. From our end on the campaign trail, my team and I make it a point to input all of our donation and expense information weekly. …
